newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Investment, riots lay bare two worlds in Argentina.
newsitem.headline: Investment, riots lay bare two worlds in Argentina.

text.p: President Carlos Menem's boast that Argentina is in "better shape than ever" has been backed up by a flurry of foreign investment. But an outbreak of protests has made it clear not everyone agrees.

The unemployed of Jujuy province, who set up 21 roadblocks to demand work and clashed with police, are back in their shanty towns watching the trucks trundle past, just like Menem's economic "miracle" has passed them by.

In towns where unemployment can reach 40 percent versus the national 17.3 percent rate, they celebrated the government's recent promise of 12,000 low-paid, short-term jobs and unemployment payments of $150 a month and lined up at dawn to put down their names for one of the precious jobs.

There have been celebrations of a different sort in Buenos Aires' financial district, where foreign banks have gone on a spending spree and invested over $2 billion toward purchasing stakes in Argentine banks in just two weeks.

For economist Mercedes Marco del Pont of the FIDE group of analysts, the Jujuy roadblocks and similar scenes in Salta, Neuquen and Cordoba provinces, and the flood of capital into Buenos Aires, "are the two faces of the economic model."

"There is a concentration of wealth and high profitability in specific market niches, generating a boom feeling, going hand-in-hand with the exclusion of some people and of the regional economies. The country is more and more divided," Marco said.
But financial markets and investors are unshaken by disturbances in the provinces and by separate riots involving students and workers in Buenos Aires and nearby La Plata.

"On the one hand, you have high jobless rates and unrest in Jujuy. But at the same time, you have big investments coming in," said Esteban Thomsen, chief Argentine economist at ING Barings. "Direct investors are saying they are not worried about social unrest. Buying a bank is a long-term investment."

Bankers like Enrique Ruete Aguirre, head of Grupo Roberts, which was bought recently by banking giant HSBC Holdings Plc, believe such business "is the best way we businessmen can help with Argentina's serious social problems."
The government believes growth along the lines of the 6.0 percent forecast for 1997 is the key to fighting unemployment, which was just 6 percent when the Peronists came to power in 1989.
But the riots' ferocity, with 180 people hurt in Jujuy in mid-May, have overshadowed euphoria over foreign investment and growth.
"There is almost abnormal concern about social problems among businessmen," said economist Ricardo Lopez Murphy.
While Menem blames protests on "subversives" ahead of October elections for Congress, even the International Monetary Fund is now warning him to heed the disturbances.

IMF chief Michel Camdessus warned the Peronist leader his reforms "could turn to failure if efforts are not intensifed to reduce the inequality in income and even more importantly, to create more opportunities for the underprivileged."
For political analyst Enrique Zuleta Puceiro, the foreign investment boom means "people can see an opulent Argentina, with a fantastic performance, which they will never attain."

In the early years of reforms led by ex-Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, the poor believed the end of hyperinflation and return to growth meant they would eventually get a slice of the cake. "Now many believe Argentina may forge ahead without them," said Zuleta Puceiro.

Economist Miguel Angel Broda, writing in El Cronista, said that since 1974 the poorest 30 percent of society has seen its income drop 25 percent while the richest 10 percent's income has grown 31.5 percent. From 1994-96, the poorest 30 percent's income shrank 10.7 percent.
"What use is price stability if its consequences are more unemployment, poverty and inequality?" asked Broda, usually a keen defender of the free-market reforms espoused by Menem.
Politicians and economists predict the roadblocks will crop up again across the country before October elections.
But Raul Buonuome, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said markets have taken as a positive signal the fact that the unrest in Jujuy was eventually resolved by dialogue.
"It had no impact on markets because they see a society that has the capacity to absorb these situations ... with much more maturity than 15 years ago," said Buonuome.
